description:
24&28 is a two-person team driven by curiosity, innovation, and a shared passion for space exploration and technology.

Our mission is to transform complex scientific challenges into accessible, meaningful, and practical digital solutions.

Participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to combine artificial intelligence, scientific research, data analysis, and modern software development to address real-world challenges in lunar exploration.

Two minds. One mission. Beyond boundaries.
summary:
At the Moon’s south pole, choosing a landing site requires more than finding suitable terrain. Sunlight, Earth visibility, and operation timing can determine whether mission requirements are met.

**Lunar Landing Site Navigator**, developed by Team 24&28, is an interactive research prototype that transforms NASA SPICE geometry and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA elevation data into an explainable lunar mission-planning workflow.

Users select landing coordinates, mission requirements, UTC start times, and operation durations. Our Python/FastAPI scientific backend evaluates terrain-aware Sun and Earth visibility, while interactive 3D lunar visualizations, local horizon views, and A/B comparisons make the results understandable.

Our **Local and Temporal Optimizers** evaluate nearby landing locations and alternative operation times, helping users identify options that better satisfy modeled mission conditions. Source-traceable results and an offline Recorded Evidence mode support transparent exploration.

By connecting NASA scientific data with actionable comparisons, our project supports accessible lunar mission-planning research and education while clearly documenting scientific limitations.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator — Team 24&28

The Challenge

Selecting a location for a lunar surface mission involves more than identifying a point on a map. Near the Moon's south pole, surrounding terrain can obstruct sunlight and Earth visibility, while changes in operation timing can significantly affect mission conditions.

Our goal was to make these complex relationships understandable, measurable, and explorable through an interactive research prototype.

Our Solution

Lunar Landing Site Navigator combines NASA scientific data, computational analysis, and interactive 3D visualization to help users investigate potential lunar landing locations and operation times.

Users can select lunar coordinates, choose from four mission profiles, specify UTC start times and operation durations, and define operational requirements.

Our scientific backend combines NASA SPICE ephemeris data with Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA elevation data to calculate Sun and Earth geometry, terrain-dependent local horizons, sampled visibility conditions, and potential operation windows.

The system evaluates whether modeled mission requirements are met and generates an explainable Planning Suitability Index. This index supports comparison but does not represent landing safety or mission success probability.

What Makes Our Project Different?

Our project goes beyond displaying the Moon or evaluating a single location.

We developed two complementary optimization systems:

Local Site Optimizer: Investigates nearby lunar coordinates, screens terrain conditions, and evaluates selected candidates to identify locations that better satisfy the defined operation requirements.

Temporal Optimizer: Keeps the selected location and mission requirements fixed while evaluating alternative UTC start times to identify potentially more favorable operation windows.

These features help answer two practical questions: Could we operate from a better nearby location? Could we achieve better conditions by changing the mission time?

In a previously executed one-hour research experiment, our Local Optimizer evaluated eight locations in detail, including the baseline. Six met the selected modeled requirements. One evaluated alternative approximately 932 meters from the baseline improved its prototype assessment from NOT_MET / 0 to MET / 100.

A separate Temporal Optimizer experiment identified two evaluated alternative start times satisfying the same example requirements. Both searches were bounded and partial; neither establishes a globally optimal solution.

Interactive Visualization

We developed the frontend using React, TypeScript, Three.js, and React Three Fiber.

The interface connects an interactive 3D lunar globe, an observer-centered local horizon visualization, Sun and Earth direction indicators, synchronized UTC exploration, a candidate radar, and A/B scenario comparisons.

These visualizations are not merely decorative. They help users understand how terrain, celestial geometry, mission requirements, and time influence modeled operational conditions.

Technical Architecture

Our backend uses Python, FastAPI, SpiceyPy, NumPy, Rasterio, and pyproj for scientific computations and geospatial processing.

We also implemented an asynchronous scientific job system with SQLite persistence, progress tracking, cancellation, and source-bound checkpoints to support long-running calculations.

A separate Recorded Evidence mode allows users to explore previously computed NASA-derived results without running the scientific backend. Recorded demonstrations are clearly distinguished from new live calculations.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Our project aims to make NASA's scientific datasets more accessible to students, researchers, and people exploring lunar mission planning.

Its main contribution is connecting scientific evidence to understandable decisions: users can examine a location, understand why modeled requirements succeed or fail, investigate alternatives, and compare results while retaining the assumptions and limitations behind each calculation.

Throughout development, we prioritized data provenance, scientific transparency, explicit operational requirements, unknown-data handling, computational efficiency, and accessible interaction.

Scientific Responsibility

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a working research prototype, not certified mission-planning or landing-safety software.

Independent absolute terrain registration and configuration-equivalent JPL Horizons validation remain incomplete. Sampled visibility does not guarantee continuous sunlight, electrical power generation, or a functioning radio link.

By making these limitations explicit, we demonstrate how open NASA data, scientific software, and interactive visualization can form a foundation for more transparent and accessible lunar exploration research.

Team 24&28 — Explore the Moon. Evaluate the Conditions. Find a Better Site.
